text.p: French drinks group Remy-Cointreau reported an 81 percent drop in 1996/97 first-half pre-tax profit on Tuesday after recording lower exceptional gains related to a prior debt restructuring.

Remy, best known for its Remy Martin cognacs, Krug and Piper-Heidsieck champagnes and Cointreau liqueurs, said pre-tax attributable income for the six months to September 30 fell to 41 million francs ($7.8 million) from 215 million in the year-earlier period.

Its pre-tax, pre-exceptional loss shrank to one million francs from 39 million francs, and Remy said it expected the improving trend to be helped by a "satisfying" level of activity seen at the start of the second half begun in October.

"As in each year, the second half is determining for the full-year results. The start of the second half has registered a satisfying level of activity which should support the improvement in the pre-tax, pre-exceptional result," it said in its first-half earnings statement.
Turnover rose four percent to 3.07 billion francs in the first half on a three percent increase in volumes sold, after a rebound in the second quarter from a weak first quarter.
Managing Director Marc Heriard Dubreuil said cognac sales in Japan were still falling but a slide in cognac sales in China, where Remy is a market leader, halted at mid-year.

"Our (cognac) sales are more difficult in Europe, in Britain and France," he told a news conference. "The economic climate in Europe isn't conducive to spending for expensive drinks," he said, but added that sales were strong in the United States.

The company's biggest brands have resumed growth, he said, and Remy is focusing on developing its distribution network for other brands, most recently through an agreement to sell Seagram liquors in the luxury holiday resort of Barbados.

Operating profit fell to 210 million francs in the first half from 216 million in the year-earlier period. The decline partly reflected a 60 million franc rise in promotional expenses to develop Remy-Cointreau brands, the company said.
The results also reflected a drop in exceptional gains -- 44 million for the first half compared with 257 million a year earlier -- due essential to a restructuring of part of the debt.
Remy's financial expense narrowed to 211 million francs from 255 million, helped by a reduction in debt to just over six billion francs at the end of the 1995/96 year.
The share price ended up 0.7 percent at 138 francs as the results were not as poor as some investors had anticipated, but analysts remained cautious about the company's prospects.
"Even if they show mechanical improvements, they haven't arrived at reducing their debt...and their operating results are not improving," one analyst said.

Marc Heriard Dubreuil said debt rose to above seven billion francs in the first half due in part to seasonal factors such as the stocks buildup ahead of the peak selling season and the May acquisition of champagne house De Venoge for 35 million francs.

"We are studying eventual asset sales," said the other managing director, Francois Heriard Dubreuil. "If they were carried out before March 31, it would have an immediate impact in the debt but we prefer to do them at the best prices."
Company officials said the debt/equity ratio at the end of the first half was roughly two to one. ($ = 5.260 French Francs)
